title: Health inequality is produced through the distribution of housing, work, money, power, public services, and protection
source_unit: World Health Organization, World report on social determinants of health equity
geography: Global; comparative evidence and country examples across high-, middle-, and low-income settings

observations.period: 2025 global health-equity assessment; social determinants and life expectancy

denominator.unit: global population and cross-country health-equity evidence base

life_expectancy_gap.unit: years between the average life expectancy in the highest- and lowest-life-expectancy countries

low_income_child_mortality_multiplier.unit: times higher likelihood of dying before age five for children born in low-income versus high-income countries

wealth_inequality_earnings_ratio.unit: times: top 10% versus bottom 50% of individual earners across 201 countries

children_saved_if_wealth_inequality_elim.unit: potential annual child lives saved by eliminating wealth-related inequality within low- and middle-income countries

observations.method: WHO global report synthesizing evidence reviews, commissioned papers, scientific and policy advisory input, country examples, and Member State consultation; it organizes 14 recommendations across four action areas.
observations.uncertainty: The report synthesizes heterogeneous evidence and policy examples; reported gaps and modeled potentials do not imply that any single intervention will produce the stated change everywhere or that social determinants operate independently.
observations.subgroup: Populations differentiated by place, income and wealth, education, race and ethnicity, gender, disability, Indigenous status, migration and access to power, money and resources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Health-care access, genetics, personal behavior and local adaptation still matter; the report’s argument is that these do not explain away the larger structural distribution of opportunity and exposure.

observations.period: 2025; fiscal capacity, social protection, discrimination, climate, conflict, and displacement

social_protection_gap.unit: people worldwide described as lacking social-protection coverage

women_without_equal_economic_opportunity.unit: women of working age described as lacking equal economic opportunities

air_pollution_early_deaths.unit: early deaths each year attributed to air pollution

climate_extreme_poverty_risk.unit: additional people potentially pushed into extreme poverty by climate change by 2030

observations.method: WHO synthesis of social, economic, environmental, political and health evidence, with policy recommendations on taxation, universal public services, anti-discrimination, climate action, digital transformation, local government and community engagement.
observations.uncertainty: Counts and projections have different years, definitions and source methods; displacement, social-protection coverage and climate-poverty estimates are not interchangeable measures of individual health loss.
observations.subgroup: People lacking income security, women facing structural discrimination, migrants and displaced people, Indigenous populations, communities exposed to pollution and climate hazards, and residents of under-resourced localities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Universal services and progressive taxation are policy prescriptions, not evidence that implementation is politically feasible, fiscally sufficient, or equally effective across settings.

related_sources.claim: Canonical WHO publication page with date, scope, recommendations and evidence basis.

boundary: This record adds a global structural-health-equity route connecting material conditions, social protection, discrimination, climate, conflict, displacement and public-service capacity to health and life chances. It is an evidence synthesis, not respondent-level ingestion, a single-country causal estimate, a clinical study, or proof that any recommendation has been implemented.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official WHO publication page, thematic page, and report PDF were reviewed; publication date, global gaps, structural determinants, social-protection and climate/displacement figures, and policy action areas were cross-checked.
